programme: A HIF1A-centered hypoxia/oxidative-stress adaptation module: HDAC7 sits directly upstream of HIF1A among its own target genes; PARK7 (DJ-1) is a known stabiliser of HIF1A and driver of the Nrf2/antioxidant-response-element programme, sharing the ARE gene NQO1 with NRF1; NRF1 runs the mitochondrial-biogenesis arm of the same stress response (TFAM, TFB2M, COX17, CYCS) alongside antioxidant genes (NQO1, GCLC, GSS); and GTF3A's own target list in this network is dominated by canonical HIF1A-inducible genes (VEGFA, KDR, EPO, ADM, NPPB, PDGFA), placing it downstream of or parallel to the same axis.
role_in_a: In cardiovascular disease, HIF1A-driven hypoxic signalling underlies ischemic injury, atherosclerotic plaque hypoxia and endothelial dysfunction; its target genes here (VEGFA, KDR, EPO, ADM) drive compensatory angiogenesis and NPPB is the transcript for BNP, a direct marker of cardiac stress. Mitochondrial and antioxidant reprogramming (NRF1, PARK7-linked NQO1/GCLC/GSS) buffers the ROS load of ischemic and failing myocardium/vasculature.
role_in_b: In liver cancer, tumour-core hypoxia and the angiogenic switch (VEGFA/KDR/EPO) are established drivers of hepatocellular carcinoma growth and a target of anti-angiogenic therapy, while HIF-stabilising and mitochondrial-reprogramming activity (PARK7, NRF1) support the metabolic adaptation of tumour cells to a hypoxic, ROS-rich microenvironment.
shared_axis: Both tissues experience localized hypoxia — ischemic vascular/cardiac tissue in cardiovascular disease, a hypoxic tumour core in hepatocellular carcinoma — and would independently recruit the same generic HIF1A-stabilisation/mitochondrial-antioxidant adaptation, explaining why the same small module recurs across patient groups from both diseases without either disease having caused it in the other.
reasoning: The programme is nameable from the target identities alone (HIF1A, VEGFA/KDR/EPO/ADM, NQO1/GCLC shared between PARK7 and NRF1), and hypoxia signalling is separately textbook-established in both ischemic cardiovascular disease and hepatocellular carcinoma, which is what 'supported' requires. But nothing in the retrieved record independently places these factors in either disease — Open Targets is empty for all twelve factors and no literature was retrieved — so the account rests on the target-gene identities and general biology rather than on anything found for this pair, which caps the strength at weak.
how_to_falsify: In a hypoxic hepatocyte line and an ischemic endothelial/cardiomyocyte model, knock down PARK7 and NRF1 and check whether HIF1A protein stabilization and induction of the shared/adjacent targets (NQO1, GCLC, VEGFA, TFAM) are lost in both tissue contexts; if HIF1A stabilization and its target induction are unaffected by PARK7/NRF1 loss in either tissue, or if HDAC7 shows no ChIP occupancy near HIF1A regulatory regions in ischemic myocardium or HCC tissue, the proposed shared hypoxia module does not hold.
caveats: Only 2 independent cohort pairs underlie the 80 patient-group comparisons, so the concordance counts (up to 50/80) likely reflect correlated subgroup splits within those 2 pairs rather than 80 independent replications. Open Targets records no curated association for any of the twelve factors with either disease, and literature retrieval returned nothing under the initial search terms — the reader's note explicitly flags that alternate disease-name searches have not yet been tried, so this absence should be read as a search-scope limitation, not as evidence the connection is novel. Only 4 of the 12 concordant factors (HDAC7, PARK7, NRF1, GTF3A) fit this account; the remaining 8, including the single highest-recurrence factor PITX1 (50/80), are developmental, cell-cycle or circadian regulators with no clear tie to hypoxia or to each other, and are deliberately left out rather than forced into the story. Tissue pairing is blood/vasculature vs. liver, both plausible sites of hypoxic stress but structurally very different, which is itself the basis for treating this as a generic shared stress pathway rather than a disease-specific mechanism.
